bart-philips-strasburg-1881-06-06.A1: FIRE.—The large stables in rear of Welsh's Hotel in this place were fired last Monday night about 10 o'clock. Although there were many people on the streets and some only a few yards from the building when the alarm was given, it was almost impossible to enter the buildings and remain long enough to save any of the property. Besides the two stables, a reaper, rake, drill, harness, ploughs, and other agricultural implements, and about five thousand shingles were burned. Fortunately the night was still and damp, as on account of the position of other buildings it would have been almost impossible to have saved the town under other circumstances. The fire company was on hand promptly, but was somewhat delayed by confusion resulting from the magnitude of the fire, and the fact that the company is so seldom called out by the alarm of fire that the discipline necessary for prompt and effective action was lacking. After these delays, the fire company did most efficient service. They had scarcely commenced work before it was evident that the company was master of the situation and there was no further fear of a general conflagration. Seyeral of our citizens distinguished themselves by their presence of mind and effective work. Lieut. Gatewood was burned about the face and suffered from a sprain of his ankle. Mr. John Knight had one foot injured. Mr. John Keller and Mr. Robt. Koontz had their hands badly burned. It was evident that the fire was the work of an incendiary. A negro by the name of Bart Philips was seen in the neighborhood of the stables and his conduct was very suspicious. Strong circumstantial evidence indicated his guilt. As soon as the fire was subdued a party was formed for the purpose of hanging Philips. The indignation of the people was such that Philips owes his life to the fortunate circumstances that kept him out of the reach of the enfiuriated crowd of citizens. He was quietly arrested and committed to jail, and every precaution necessary to secure him was taken. He was brought before Justice Rodeffer yesterday and committed for indictment. There was no insurance on the property.

NEW YORK, August 26th.—Public sympathy runs decidedly with the young California lady who chastised the self-styled British Captain Burslem at West Point, for the reason that the immediate provocation for her impulsive act was only the culmination of a persistent series of unmanly and exasperating annoyances previously sustained at his hands. RETIREMENT OF SURGEONS. Woodward: Reyburn and Barnes Retire from President's Case.
At a late hour to-night the agent of the National Associated Press received definite information that the rumors about the retirement of three of the physicians from the president's case were about to be confirmed. The information came direct from those most interested, and cannot be mistaken. Drs. Barnes, Woodward and Reyburn signed the bulletin to-night for the last time, and to-morrow the early bulletin will contain the official announcement of the fact that hereafter Dr. Bliss will have full control of the case with Drs. Agnew and Hamilton consulting physicians. One of them is to be with Dr. Bliss all the time. Intimations of such an occurrence have been given from time to time, but it was not until to-night that the fact was in any way established. Dr. Bliss stated that the change was made in deference to the wish of the president and not on account of any difference between the physicians in the case. He did not think the president had any particular reason for dsiring such a change beyond a wish to have fewer attendants and more quiet. "Sickmen's wishes," said Dr. Bliss, "are not always easily explained."

Further inquiry to-night shows the facts to be about as follows: On Saturday last the event of the project of the journey was being definitely considered. The president said to Mrs. Garfield: "What is the use of all the physicians going to Long Branch?" The remark so impressed Mrs. Garfield that she mentioned it to one of the physicians, and they talked it over together. Meanwhile the president had said that he thought Dr. Bliss will be enough to take care of him, with Dr Agnew and Dr. Hamilton. to consult with him. Under the circumstances it was particularly referred to Dr. Agnew for his advice. He, in turn, thought that the physicians the president proposed to eliminate ought to be the ones to speak. Dr. Woodward, it seems, was anxious to retire and both Drs. Reyburn and Surgeon General Barnes had business in Washington which they could ill afford to neglect. So the arrangement above referred to was made.

All the streams and ponds in Ocean and Monmouth counties are dried up and the spring are giving out. Wood fires in Alsion, Shamony and Whitings are spreading with alarming rapidity and only copious showers will stop the work of destruction.

Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune,
Rico, Colo., Sept. 10. About 9:30 last Sunday evening the closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy was played at Silverton, thirty-five miles northeast of here. Some days before a promiscuous shooting-match had occurred in a saloon several miles north of Durango, on the Durango and Silverton toll-road. During the molle the salookeeper was killed, but no one know who fired the fatal shot. Hert Wilkinson and a "coon" named Jim Catrin, both of whom had figured prominently in the row, immediately made themselves scarce, and shortly afterwards turned up, in company with Dison Eskridge, on the streets of Silverton. Eskridge, who had been here for some time attending to mining interests, had started for Durango the morning of the day on which the shooting occurred. It is claimed that he was not present when the saloonkeeper was killed. The Marshal of Silverton, Clate Ogsbury, attempted to arrest the party, and was

KILLED ALMOST INSTANTLY, living only long enough to state that Wilkinson was the one to whom he owed his death.

The three at once fled, but nearly 100 men were upon their track within a few minutes. Catrin was caught the next day and lodged in the Silverton Jail, from which he was taken the same evening and lynch law most effectively dealt out to him. A reward of $5,500 was offered for the delivery, dead or alive, to the Sheriff of San Juan County, of Wilkinson and Eskridge. The latter is still at liberty. The former was captured by the notorious Ike Stockton, for whom Wilkinson would have risked his life at any time, of which fact Stockton was perfectly aware. The following account of the capture was given by Mrs. Flora W. Pyle, the sister of Wilkinson, who resides at Castle Rock Springs. The statement of Mrs. Pyle was taken verbatim by a special reporter of the Dolores News, and is the only true and accurate account yet given:

"My brother (A. W. Wilkinson) and Dison Eskridge came to our house at 12 o'clock at night on Sunday. They knocked at the door gently, and I answered the call, asking who was there. The answer was, 'Bert.' When I recognized Bert his first words were: 'Flora, we are awful hungry, but have you got anything that will fit Dison's feet; he is barefooted. He then asked if I had anything cooked. I gave them a lunch, which they ate outdoors. They did not enter the house during the time they were hereabouts.

LATEST NEWS
—A London dispatch states that France and England have agreed on an Anglo-French military commission for the reorganization of the Egyptian army so as to prevent future annoyance to either nation.

—John W. Brooks, of Boston, the famous railroad manager, died at Heidelberg, Germany, in his 63d year. He constructed the Boston and Maine road, negotiated the purchase of the Michigan Central by Boston capitalists, built various sections of the Burlington road, and was Chairman of the Hoosac tunnel commission.

—Dr. Lugenbeel, a brother of Mrs. Christiancy, sent a formal challenge to the ex-Minister, which was declined, and a warrant asked for. The cause was reflections upon her testimony in the divorce suit.

—Portions of Iowa, Minnesota, Michigan and Nebraska, were visited by a slight snow-fall on the 16th of September.

—The New York Prohibitionists have nominated a full ticket for State officers, to be voted for at the November election.

—The value of buildings erected in Chicago, so far this year, approximates $10,275,000.

—Wheat along the Canadian Pacific road in Manitoba is said to average fully twenty-five bushels per acre, oats sixty and barley thirty.

—The Department of Agriculture reports the general average of the potato crop in the seven chief States at 68.

—Dr. Hutchinson, of Fulton county, Ark., went down into a well on his premises for the purpose of cleaning it out, and was overcome by foul air. A neighbor, while in the act of descending to his assistance, fell to the bottom of the well and broke his neck. A second neighbor descended the deadly pit and he, too, was overcome by and died from the effects of the foul gases. A number of persons, attracted by the frantic cries of Mrs. Hutchinson, gathered at the spot, and the bodies of the three dead men were taken from the well. To cap the climax of the horror, Mrs. Hutchinson has gone crazy with grief.

- Nearly $150,000 worth of property has been swept away by fire at East Rome, N. Y.

- A west-bound train from Vicksburg, Miss., ran off the track near Edwards' Depot. A sleeping-car, a passenger car and a Superintendent's car were wrecked. Many passengers were injured, six rather seriously.

- Bert Wilkinson, who during the past year killed no less than three men, was lynched at Silverton, Col.

- A negro woman was roasted alive at Dyke's Mills, La., by a mob of citizens, for having murdered two little children.

- The residence of Mrs. Jane Shiers, near Gastonia, N. C., was blown up by dynamite while she was absent. Charles Deplace, a discarded paramour, is believed to have perpetrated the deed, in the hope of extinguishing a rival.

Guiteau, it seems from late news from Washington, is consumed with a horrible dread and fear since he has discovered in the papers, he was allowed to read the sentiment of the people toward him.

John Morrissey, an old man, a farmer living near Burlingame, Kansas, was stopped a few evenings ago near his house, while feeding his cattle, and robbed by four masked men. He lost $1,550 which he had in his pocket.
One day last week, Miss Addie Fox, daughter of Mr. George Fox, one of the most prominent citizens of Suscola, Illinois, and a young man named John Sands, 20 years of age, a farm hand living in the neighborhood, quietly eloped and going to Louisville, Kentucky, were married.

Alabama is to have a new railroad, as declarations of incorporation have been filed with the secretary of state of that state, for the Warrior Coalfield railroad, to run from Decatur to Gainesville, tapping the finest coal mines and running through some of the finest cotton and timber lands in the state.

A man named Jesse Franklin, living near Monroe, Louisiana, was hunting hogs a few days ago, and finding one he wanted, shot and killed it, but unfortunately killed two of a neighbor's children with the same shot. A coroners inquest acquitted Franklin of any intentional wrong, as the children were not in sight when he fired.

A dastardly crime, one that should be visited with the most condign punishment of the law, was committed near Dubuque, Iowa, a few nights ago, upon a young man named Powers. He was married that evening, and during the night a charivari party visited the house, but not meeting with any response to their hideous serenade, one of the party thrust a shotgun into a window and, firing it off, wounded young Powers seriously in the breast and left arm.

A few days ago at Joplin, Missouri, an old man named McCall, was driving a spirited team of horses, hitched to a farm, wagon, and a passing team frightened them causing them to run away. The body of the wagon was thrown off seriously injuring the old man. The team ran on and, colliding with a small building, the tongue of the wagon was driven through the side of the house, passing just over a bed on which a sick woman lay. The escape of the woman from death or serious injury was miraculous.

Independence, Missouri, has been greatly exercised for a week past over the mysterious appearance of blood-red seals, with cabalistic characters in black ink upon them. These seals are placed on the houses of those who have taken any active interest in the arrest and trial of the train robbers. We rather suspect some of the boys are having a little fun at the expense of the credulous and timid. However, the officers are on the alert, and are making every endeavor to discover the perpetrators of the joke or warning, as the case may be. The actual train robbers hardly have time for such foolishness.

Two men, named John Reynolds and Robert Edwards, were arrested a day or two ago at Boonville on suspicion of stealing a watch from the Missouri Pacific railroad depot at Smithton. They were searched unsuccessfully in the telegraph office in Boonville, but during the search Reynolds, who had the watch, succeeded in concealing it in a box of waste paper in the telegraph office. They were taken to the Sedalia jail and locked up in separate cells, when Edwards confessed that Reynolds had shown him the watch and told him where he concealed it. A telegram to Boonville caused a search for the box and the watch was found.

Frank Pollock, a hard working and much respected farmer, living some ten miles from Hot Springs, Arkansas, was shot and instantly killed by a young man named John Colburn, a few days ago. Pollock's wife had formerly been the wife of Colburn, having borne him two bright children, but domestic troubles ensuing, they separated and the wife obtained a divorce, marying Pollock afterwards. Colburn, when he learned of the marriage wrote Pollock word that he intended to have his children and kill him, and accordingly accompanied by two friends went to Pollock's and commenced abusing him and opened fire on him, which Pollock returned, breaking Colburn's arm; Colburn however, succeeded in killing Pollock and with his children and two friends departed for parts unknown. Colburn is reported to be a hard character
Mr. James Wallace, a planter in Stone county, Arkansas, employed, a short time since, a young man named George Gray, to superintend his cotton crop, that is, the gathering thereof. Gray is a handsome young man, and of most pleasant address, and directly a friendly relationship was established between him and Mrs. Wallace, a young and beautiful woman. This intimacy terminated a few days ago in the flight of Gray and Mrs. Wallace. The two left in a canoe down the river, intending to take rail at the nearest station: Wallace discovered the flight, and arming himself with a shot-gun, started in hot pursuit in a skiff and soon came up with the fugitives and opened fire on Gray, who made reply with a pistol, and thus they fought a duel down the river, the wife guiding Gray's boat while he sent broadsides at her husband, until both boats were disabled and drifted to opposite sides of the river. Gray and the wife abandoned their boat and pursued their flight through the woods, and Wallace organized aa posse to follow them, swearing vengeance on Gray for desecrating the sanctity of his home.

Shooting Cases in Baltimore.
BALTIMORE, July 4.—Several cases of shooting have occurred in this city to-day. A difficulty occurred in South Baltimore between whites and blacks, in which William Hecker, a white man who was near, was shot, and his life is despaired of. Thomas H. Ross, colored, was arrested on the charge of shooting him. Isaac Curtis, colored, who was engaged in the affray was shot, and his wound is thought to be mortal. In the northern section of the city Miss Mary F. Geblin was looking from a second-story window, when John Carr, aged 17, fired upward and the ball from his pistol entered one of her eyes and killed her. Several other persons were shot, but as far as can be learned none seriously.

A FRENCH OPINION Of the American Constitution Not Without Interest.
PARIS, July 4.—Le Temps in discussing the ultimate consequences to the United States, should President Garfield die, remarked: "How greatly the rigidity of American constitutional institutions, which are based on the absolute principle of separating the powers of the legislature from those of the executive, and on the mutual independence of the President and Congress, multiplies the chances of conflict, which can only be solved after the expiration of a fixed term; whereas, the English parliamentary system of responsible government settles the difficulties by an appeal to the people, or by a modification of the ministry."

GLADSTONE

On the Attempt upon the Life of President Garfield.

LONDON, July 4.—Mr. Gladstone's statement in the House of Commons to-day, respecting the attempt on President Garfield's life, was as follows: "We cannot be surprised that the question has arisen in regard to the inspiration of the outrage upon President Garfield, the character of which is such as to attract the attention of the whole civilized world, and which so greatly affects the feelings and welfare of a nation which is not only friendly to us, but which is growing more friendly yearly. The public has been supplied with extraordinary rapidity with information of all the fluctuations in the terrible trial which the President has been called upon to undergo."

In the House of Lords Earl Granville said the sympathy of all classes in England was increased every hour, and that it was not less strong than that felt in America itself.

SEVEN PERSONS KILLED

And a Dozen Wounded Through a Forgetful Engineer.

CINCINNATI, July 4.—Seven persons were killed and twelve others wounded by an accident on the Kentucky Central railroad, twelve miles south of Covington, this afternoon about three o'clock. All were residents of Covington. The names of the killed are: John Rye, Michael Dixon, William Callopy William Wiechouf, John Caller, and two boys, names unknown, who were stealing a ride. John Rye was a fireman, the others were passengers. The wounded are: George Callopy, both legs broken and otherwise bruised; John Carney, nose and face badly bruised; Mrs. Brown, leg broken; Paul Sheridan bruised badly; John McDonald, left leg and collar-bone broken; John Rush, leg broken; John Cochran, left arm broken and scalded; Maggie Carey, scalded badly; James Crow, bruised internally; John Bethel, bruised leg and knee; Ed Hayne, cheek cut. It was a collision of the south-bound Lexington express with a picnic excursion, which was backing north for another load. The train-dispatcher ordered Conductor Frank Matlock to side-track at Culbertson Station and let the picnic train pass. The conductor gave the orders to Jake Matlock, engineer, who forget them, and passed the station. The collision was in a deep curved cut. Both the locomotives are a total wreck.

GRAIN IN EUROPE.

Weekly Review of the Foreign Breadstuffs Markets.

LONDON, July 4.—The Mark Lane Express in its review of the grain trade for the past week, says the weather has been uninterruptedly fine and wheat has passed through the critical blossoming period favorably. In regard to barley, appearances indicate a good crop on the best land and variable elsewhere. The oats prospect is bad, and appears to be the worst. Regarding trade, on account of scarcity, native wheats advanced both in London and the

provinces, and the advance was maintained, but at the close buyers operated less freely. Foreign trade has been of the wane the whole week. Wheat, on Friday, was cheaper all round. The advance which was screwed out Monday was due to the small supply. This advance was lost, particularly regarding American red winter on spot. The decline amounted to 6d@1s, yet buyers hesitated. The amount on passage increased the week's supply, chiefly Indian, Russian and American. Flour maintains Monday's advance, but the demand, which has been only consumptive, is slackening. The foreign supply, chiefly Australian and European, is very large. Prices were lower it London and the provinces on Friday. Barkey was dull and rates lower where business was transacted. Oats, native and foreign, firm and dearer. Maize quiet in tone and in buyers' favor. Sales of English wheat the past week, 19,371 quarters, against 17,974 the corresponding week last year.

TUPELO, MISS.

Proceedings of the Lee County Democratic Convention.

Special to the Appeal.]

TUPELO, Miss., July 4.—The Lee county Democratic Convention met here to-day. They indorsed Senator Lamar unanimously, recommended him as his own successor, and unanimously instructed for J. M. Stone for Governor, and for J. A. Kincanon for Auditor. They expressed profound regret at the attempted assassination of the President, and sympathy for him, and an earnest hope for his speedy recovery.

JACKSON, TENN.

Meeting of Citizens—Resolutions of Sorrow and Sympathy.

Special to the Appeal.]

JACKSON, July 4.—The news of the attempt to assassinate President Garfield created a profound sensation among all classes of people here. A large meeting of citizens of the city and county assembled at the Courthouse this evening and passed resolutions expressing sorrow and sympathy for President Garfield and family.

The following account of the murder of William L. Hoblitzell, formerly of this county, and the lynching of the murderer is taken from the Cumberland Daily News: CAMP HOBLITZELL, COL., Oct. 27, '81.

At or about the hour of nine o'clock this morning, while Mr. W. L. Hoblitzell was engaged in business at camp 5, one Ben, or as he was commonly called, Pete Theophil, know on the roll of his works as Italian No. 61, approached him and in an excited manner, and in broken English, demanded his pay as he intended to leave. It being Mr. Hoblitzell's rule to pay only after ten day's notice, excepting, of course, the regular monthly pay days, he told Ben that he could not get his money until pay day, unless he had given the usual notice. This Ben knew very well, as he had been employed there for several months, but it did not satisfy him, and he repeated his demand in a manner usually violent. Mr. Mr. Hoblitzell did not understand all Ben said, as most of it was spoken in Italian, but I never saw him more mild and gentle in manner.

After a few minutes, and when he had finally told Ben that the rule applied to all without exception, he came into the office and was for some time engaged with myself in the examination of papers. The Italian continued to talk outside, and finally came into the store adjoining the office. Then Mr. Hoblitzell told him to leave or he would put him out. Ben stubbornly refused to go, and in the effort to eject him a desperate struggle took place in which Ben was decidedly getting the worst, when I summoned a colored man to help, and we separated them, Ben agreeing to go, and passing out the door. In a moment, and before it can be described, he turned stepped on the sill of the door and fired at Mr. Hoblitzell, who was only a few paces from him, and was apparently adjusting his clothing, which had become disarranged in the struggle.

After firing, the Italian ran, brandishing his revolver and threatening a man who attempted to stop him. In the excitement incident to the shooting the would be murderer escaped, and up to the hour of writing (2 p. m.) has eluded pursuit. Mr. Hoblitzell is of vigorous physique and possesses a strong constitution, which may materially assist in his recovery, but the wound is a serious dne, the ball entering the right breast an inch below and to the right of the nipple.

T. F. McCARDELL.

The wife of Mr. Hoblitzell, who was at Colorado Springs, was telegraphed for, and she and her daughter left there at 7:30 p. m. on a special train furnished by the railroad company. No mention is being made of their having reached Camp Hoblitzell, before the death of Mr. Hoblitzell, which occurred at 9 p. m., just twelve hours after he was shot.

Specials from Gunnison to the Denver Republican state that a reward of $1,000 was offered for the capture of Theophil, and that the sheriff and a hundred men—principally the railroad laborers who had been working for Mr. Hoblitzell—overtook him in the mountains, and brought him to Gunnison, Friday evening.

Fearing an outbreak the prisoner was removed from the jail to the court house where a better guard could be kept over him, and a strong guard stationed there. At midnight, however, masked men appeared and covered the guards with guns and pistols, while others rushed in, placed a rope around the Italian s neck, dragged him down the stair steps, then through the snow a distance of two squares, and then hanged him to a livery stable sign, where he was found Saturday morning.

THE MURDER OF COL. KOBLITZELL.
COL. W. H. HOBLITZELL was a contractor on the Denver and Rio Grande railroad with his camp and workmen in Black Canon, Gunnison county, Colorado. He was a resident of Ursina, Somerset county, Pa., and formerly a contractor on the Pittsburg and Connellsville railroad.

An Italian, who demanded his pay, called at the tent of Col. W. H. Hoblitzell in the Black Canon, on Tuesday morning, Oct. 27, and got into an altercation with that gentleman, the result was that the Italian was very severely pounded. He then left Col. Hoblitzell's tent and, procuring a pistol, returned and shot the contractor, inflicting a wound from which his victim died on Thursday night.

The story of the pursuit and capture of the Italian is a thrilling one and reads with all the interest of a western novel.

Col. Hoblitzell was shot early on Thursday morning. At eight o'clock that evening Sheriff Yule reached the camp. His horse was smoking from the hard ride, and he exchanged it for a sure footed and tolerably fleet mule. Col. Hoblitzell was alive when the sheriff reached the scene of the tragedy, but he died shortly afterwards.

The first move of the sheriff's was to hunt up from the men employed at the camp a couple of honest and faithful fellows, who knew the Italian and could be counted upon to stand by and aid him. The task was not a difficult one—Col. Hoblitzell being popular among his men, and a hundred hot-blooded fellows were eager to accompany the sheriff in the pursuit of the Italian. The sheriff selected Peter Smith and A. S. Albright, and just before nine o'clock on Thursday evening left the camp, keeping to the west down the canon. Smith, who is a young man of undoubted courage, and who swore by all that was holy that he would catch the murderer or never return to camp, rode a small sorrel pony. The sheriff and Albright were mounted on mules. The wagon road led the men from the camp across a prairie of sage brush. It was a dark night and cold, and withal a dismal ride. Trustworthy information had convinced the pursuers that the man they pursued was well armed and desperate. It was known that immediately after firing the murderous shot, he had hurried to his cabin, and taken there-from a double-barreled shot gun. This weapon, with the English bulldog with which he committed the murder, made him a formidable foe to overtake.

The new moon had set as the pursuing party left camp No. 3 and started a long and cheerless ride for the first camp in contractor Hutchinson's division. There was scarcely enough light to enable the men to see the road. When seven miles had been traveled the smouldering ashes of a camp fire were made out, close to the road on the right hand side. It immediately occurred to Smith that this fire had been kindled by the Italian, and that he could not be far distant. The three men at once reined in their animals and held a hasty consultation of war.

The smoke from the smouldering fire arose from an open garden of sage brush. The nearest timber was between a quarter and a half a mile distant. It was obvious that if the murderer lurked in the vicinity of the fire, he had his would be captors at a decided disadvantage. They knew that he was well armed and desperate. It was therfore decided, as nothing could be seen of him, to continue on down the canon to Hutching's first camp, and to return over the road in the morning. Arriving they remained in the camp not more than ten or fifteen minutes, and then remembring the smouldering fire they had seen began to retrace their steps eastward. Coming to the house of a ranchman (whose name they have forgotten or failed to learn) they applied for shelter, and upon stating their mission were well taken care of.

After a rest of three-quarters of an hour, just before daylight they were in the saddle again on their way to the fire by the roadside. Albright rode in advance, Smith rode a horse length or two behind him, and Sheriff Yule rode in the rear. The first streaks or daylight were making their appearance as the party came in sight of the camp fire by the roadside. Involuntarily they slackened their speed, and just as they did so the figure of a man was seen to descend from the left bank and move into the road. It was clearly the intention of this person to hail them, and they advanced slowly and cautiously. There was not enough light to make his features distinct, and he evidently failed to recognize the approaching horsemen, for he stood in the middle of the road, and as Albright drew up to him asked for a match. Special Dispatch to the Daily Tribune.
RUSHFORD, Minn., Sept. 15—A most horrible tragedy occurred at this place on Tuesday night. A man and daughter, George Martin, a farmer living three miles from the village, were returning from neighbors about nine o'clock in the afternoon accompanied by two sisters. As the girls were passing a ravine—they met a boy with a gun. Without warning he fired upon the party, disappearing with a yell. Anna Martin fell dead. From the uncertain description of the person who did the shooting given by the frightened girls, suspicion fell upon a Bohemian boy named Jacob Pruchker. About four o'clock next morning a party went to his home and captured him. He at first denied any knowledge of the affair, but being threatened by the party he finally confessed having done the deed. He gave no reason, and is evidently a lunatic. The boy is in custody, and threats are made to lynch him, but great precautions to prevent have been taken. The girl was of a good family and of excellent reputation.

If any one wants real choice, reasonable fish stories, he should go to Minnesota. Folks have no fancy for the incredible up there; the facts are so plenty that exaggeration is simple folly. A party of anglers were seated around in a Minnesota depot, with a fine string of fish, a few days ago, waiting for a train, and killed time by relating their experiences. What he was about to tell was true, because it had been his own experience. Alluding to some remarks that had been made about the rapid growth of fish in Minnesota waters, he said that four years ago he caught a three-pound bass. As he did not want small fish he threw the body back into the water, but before doing so, tied a little toy tin whistle to its tail. ALTON, Ill., June 16.—Last night about 10 o'clock, Owen O'Hare, one of our well-known citizens, having been engineer on the Chicago & Alton Railroad since it was built, though off duty at present owing to sickness, was shot and severely wounded. When brought into court he knocked down and kicked his wife, knocked over Judge Langlois, the magistrate, and attacked the Constable with a razor. Then the latter drew and shot him dead in his tracks.

MURDER OF A GAMBLER.

DENVER, Colo., June 10.—About noon today James Moon, a notorious gambler, was shot and instantly killed by Clay Wilson, another gambler. The shooting resulted from a quarrel about a woman. Moon had threatened Wilson's life. To-day he started to put him out of a saloon, when the latter turned and fired, producing four wounds, any one of which would have caused death.

COW-BOYS ON THE WAR-PATH.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., June 16.—A party of seventy desperate cow-boys have left Willeox, Arl., for Fronteras, on the Mexican side, to avenge the death of four Americans who were killed at that place three weeks ago. Notice has been sent to the people of Fronteras and to Mexican troops near there, and a bloody fight is expected.

SHOT BY HIS BROTHER-IN-LAW.

GEORGETOWN, Ky., June 10.—Mack Salyers, a young married man living near this town, shot his brother-in-law, John Bonnell, twice this afternoon, killing him instantly, because Bonnell treated his sister, Salyers wife, badly.

HYMENEAL.

CARLINVILLE, Ill., June 10.—Miss Minna Koester, of this city, was united in marriage to Prof. Henry Merz, of Blackburn University, at the residence of the bride's father, to-night. New Iberia Sugar Bowl: Last Monday our town was a scene of great excitement in the vicinity of Justice Langlois' office when it was learned that Constable J. M. Senac had shot and instantly killed a colored man named Jeff Hill, while on trial for beating his wife last Sunday. The facts obtained by us are as follows: During the trial of the case, Hill grew indignant over the statement made to the court by his wife and attempted a second assault upon her; refusing to obey the judge's summons to keep her quiet, Constable Senac was ordered to take him to jail. Hill was persistent in resisting the officer and, finally, making a motion as if to draw a weapon, Mr. Senac drew his revolver and fired, killing him almost instantly. Shreveport Times: For several weeks the police have been on the alert for a negro man named Willian Green, who is wanted for larceny. Last evening between 6 and 7 o'clock Policeman Wimbish got on Green's track and soon discovered him in a store near the ferry landing. The negro saw the officer approaching, broke and ran toward Jones' saw mill, and was distancing Wimbish so badly that he called to several to stop the thief, when Mr. Wiley Downs rushed out from Jones' mill and captured Green and held him until the officer arrived when he turned the prisoner over to him. No sooner was Green, who is a man of superior physical strength, in the custody of Mr. Wimbish, than he grabbed him by the throat, began chocking him and swearing at the top of his voice that there were not policemen enough in town to arrest him. Mr. Wimbish managed to get his pistol out and dealt the negro several blows over the head before he could be induced to relax his hold. Mr. Downs again came to the assistance of the officer and also another gentleman and between the three they soon secured the desperate negro. Meantime a large number of negroes had assembled and violently opposed the officer and Mr. Downs and threatened to rescue Green at all hazards, and only for the coolness and determination displayed by the white men the negroes doubtless would have carried their threats into execution. Last night Chief Austin instructed the force to arrest the ring leaders and lock them up.

This only increased his excitement and arising violently, let out a shower of curses and, advancing in a threatening way, toward the two officers, said no son of a b—— of a judge or constable would jail him. THE FIRE ENGINEERS In Convention at Richmond, Va.—Officers Elected for Next Year.
RICHMOND, September 13.—The Virginia Association of Fire Engineers held its ninth annual convention to-day. Mayor Carrington delivered the address of welcome. G. Watt Taylor, of Richmond, was elected President of the Association for next year. Among the Vice-Presidents are John Garcey, of Toledo; J. B. Palf, of Joilet; Thos. O'Neil, of Kalanazoo; J. G. THE "PEN"

Mightier Than the Policeman's Bludgeon—A Case in Point in Ohio.

Columbus, O., September 13.—A dispatch from Newark to-day says that Policeman Griffith assaulted F. Watson, one of the editors of the Newark Pen, and afterward, with Marshal Rickenbaugh, arrested and locked him up. The cause of the trouble was an item detrimental to Griffith which appeared in the Pen. F. L. Cross, a partner of Watson, was also arrested last evening on the charge of assault and battery. Both were released on their own recognizance. Officer Griffith was arrested on the affidavit of Cross, and waived an examination and was bound over to the Court in the sum of two hundred dollars. Placards comparing Cross with Guiteau were scattered over the streets in the morning. The Pen's bulletin board was thrown in the canal. Considerable excitement prevails. The dispatch says that fifty or more citizens will support the editors.

THE STRIKERS

And the Cotton Men Have Consented to Arbitration by the Chamber of Commerce.

NEW ORLEANS, September 13.—It is reported that the British Consul has asked protection for the steamships Historian and Cella, and the bark George. The Governor promised to send troops this afternoon, but none were sent. If none are sent by 10 o'clock to-morrow the Consul will communicate with the British Minister at Washington. It is also rumored that the Spanish Consul has wired the Spanish Minister at Washington, relative to affairs on the steamship Galego.

Everything is quiet to-night under the rumor generally credited, that the Cotton Men's Council and the Executive Committee of the Labor Associations have agreed to accept the arbitration of the Chamber of Commerce Committee. This committee met at 6 p.m., and before adjourning will finally decide all the issues between capital and labor.

Representatives of the Labor Council have been admitted to a conference and a tariff is under consideration.

Fires Still Raging in the Ontario Forests.

BELLEVILLE, ONT., September 13.—A large part of the timber limits on Scash river, including portions of those belonging to Rathbun & Son, Gilmore & Co., Alexander Sutherland, William Bleeker and Flint & Hatton, were devastated. Two hundred sleighs in the township of Anglesia belonging to Gilmore & Co., and their jobbers, were destroyed. Sutherland saved his sleighs, blankets, and a portion of his cooking utensils, but lost the shanties, stoves, and a large quantity of lumber. An immense quantity belonging to various other individuals was destroyed. The fires are still raging.

Two Men Killed by a Falling Building.

RICHMOND, VA., September 13.—A three-story brick building in course of erection for the Richmond and Allegheny Railroad company fell to-day and several workmen were injured, four seriously. Wm. Warren, a plumber, was killed, and his helper, Marcellus Mosley, was fatally injured. The disaster is attributed to a badly planned roof, which was crushed in by the weight of the slates.

Highwaymen in New England.

PORTLAND, September 13.—There was a family robbed while proceeding from the Glen House to the Thorn Mountain House, near the line of the Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad. Later the Glen stage-coach was fired into, but the driver whipped up the horses and escaped. Officers are searching for the highwaymen.

last Tuesday our District Court room was the theater of a thrilling scene from real life, which five minutes afterwards terminated in a tragedy. At the opening of the 'rm the grand jury indicted Josephus Fairchild for the murder of a negro named Frank Clout. Josephus was a short but strongly built negro.

The homicide was committed near Lake Charles last spring, and Josephus, after lying out a few days, went to Rapides parish, where he was arrested by the sheriff of Rapides, and lodged in jail at Alexandria. Our sheriff, being informed of the arrest, sent deputy sheriff John S. Hawkins to Alexandria, and he soon returned and lodged Josephus in jail at this place. He was tried by jury, and convicted by an unqualified verdict. Just before noon last Tuesday, by order of District Judge Hon. S. D. Read, he was brought into court to receive sentence of death, his handcuffs and shackles having been removed, as usual when prisoners are to be sentenced. As he sat down in a chair everybody could see, by the trembling of his limbs, that he was violently agitated, but by a supreme effort he controlled his features so that they presented no evidence of emotion beyond an occasional anxious glance at the open windows near by. He was attended by four deputy sheriffs, one of whom—Richard Coward—carried a Winchester rifle, the others having pistols in their hip pockets. Sentenced, in due form of law, to be hung by the neck until he was dead, a deputy sheriff took hold of the prisoner's left arm, and started to lead him out of the courtroom, the other deputies following just behind him. As he stepped on the first of the three or four steps leading from the front door to the ground, Josephus, with a single movement, threw off the grasp on his arm, and leaped around the southwest corner of the courthouse building. As he sprung across the ditch by the road side, Coward and another deputy fired almost simultaneously, and Josephus fell. Instantly rising, however, he resumed his race for life, running up the street and past the jail, amid a perfect storm of bullets, several of which perforated his shirt within an inch of his body. As he reached Ryan street he turned to the right and ran down that street. As Mr. Coward reached the same corner, and Josephus had nearly reached the next square, a ball from Mr. Coward's rifle struck the fugitive a little back of and over the left ear, glanced around the skull and came out at the face. Josephus, of course, fell headlong, and was taken up and carried to the jail, where he remained totally unconscious until between ten and eleven o'clock that night, when he expired. As the attending physician declared his skull was not factured, and as the only other wound was a flesh wound in the leg, there is no doubt he died from concussion of the brain, caused by the ball which struck his head.

An inquest was held, and the verdict of the coroner's jury justified the killing of the prisoner while under sentence of death and escaping from legal custody.

Smith, Clerk of the United States Court, had been found murdered at about 2 o'clock this morning at his office door in the third story of the United States Court-House. Col. Smith not coming home last night at the usual hour, his mother became anxious concerning him, and called on Dr. Moore, a near neighbor, to go and look for him down-town. The Doctor telephoned to druggist Kuhn about 2 o'clock to go to Col. Smith's office and see if he was there, as he had been complaining of being sick. Kuhn did so, and found Col. Smith lying dead upon the floor in the hall, in a pool of blood, with a bullet-hole in his head.

THE ALARM WAS GIVEN, and investigation was begun. A revolver of a large calibre was found sticking in his left pantaloons-leg, near the foot, with the butt-end exposed. His key was still in his door, which he was about to shut up on departing. The door was partly open. Two letters which he had written, directed, and stamped were on the floor at his feet, as they had fallen from his hand. It was apparent that he intended to mail them down-stairs in the post-office as he should leave the building. His hat was on the back of his head, full of blood. He had turned out the gas in his office, and the murderer probably turned out the gas in the hall, and laid in wait for him, and, as he was about to close his door, put a revolver to his head and fired, striking above the left temple, the ball.

LINCOLN, Neb., Nov. 5.—The news of the shooting at Omaha of Watson B. Smith, Clerk of the United States District Court, was brought into the District Court in this city this morning, and it caused a profound sensation. The Hon. T. Marquette addressed the court, and said that telegrams received from Omaha announced that Watson B. Smith had been murdered at the door of his office at Omaha. He suggested that there be a meeting of the bar of the United States Court this evening, and that his Honor preside. Mr. Marquette further remarked that Mr. Smith, in his office, had been a friend and helper of the attorneys who practiced in the United States Courts. For the past five months he had been actively engaged and endeavoring to enforce the laws in this city as well as in Omaha. Lawyers knew the necessity of enforcing the law, and the good which follows such enforcement. He hoped, therefore, every member of the bar would be present to honor the memory of one who had sacrificed his life in support of the laws of his country. In compliance with the suggestion of Mr. Marquette, a full representation of the bar of Lincoln is now in public meeting at the United States Court-House, and speeches are being made in relation to the sad affair. The people of Lincoln, and especially the legal fraternity, are horrified over the assassination. Every particular in relation to the same is eagerly caught up and discussed by our people, and the greatest sympathy is felt for the immediate friends and relatives of the deceased. Col. Smith was well known in this city, and bore the reputation of being an excellent citizen and a bold and outspoken friend of law and order.

DIED IN JAIL AT BALLSTON.
BALLSTON, N. Y., Dec. 9.—John Lyons, of No. 329 East Thirty-sixth st., New-York, who was in jail here for false pretences, died to-day.

DURFEE SENT TO JAIL.
NEWPORT, R. I., Dec. 9.—William H. Durfee, the alleged forger, having been unable to secure ball, was taken to jail to-day. The case will be presented to the Grand Jury in March.

SUICIDE OF AN INSANE MAN.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., Dec. 9.—At Newcastle, Stephen Cook has committed suicide by shooting. He was forty-five years old and had been considered deranged for some time.

A FATHER SHOOTS HIS SON.
WARREN, Ohio, Dec. 9.—M. D. Phelps shot and killed his son, William Phelps, at Bristolville, Ohio, yesterday. It was an unprovoked murder.

A NEGRO SHOT AND KILLED.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., Dec. 9.—At the Pratt Coal Mines, in Jefferson County, an officer attempted to arrest a negro, who resisted and seized a shotgun. Before he could fire, however, the officer shot him fatally.

NO INDICTMENT FOUND.
NORRISTOWN, Penn., Dec. 9.—The Grand Jury has ignored the bill against John Spellman, charged with the murder of Samuel Clugston, at Valley Forge last March.

INDICTMENTS FOR MURDER.
SPRINGFIELD, Mass., Dec. 9.—The Grand Jury today reported indictments for murder in the cases of Dwight Kidder, Jr., who shot his brother, Charles D Kidder, in this city, and Turpin Jenks, for the murder of John Otis, at Long Meadow.

SHOT BY A BURGLAR.
PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 9.—Bernard McMahon, who kept a grocery store at Eighth and Wharton-sts., was shot and almost instantly killed to night by a burglar. A young man named Wymer has been arrested on suspicion of being the murderer.

CRIME ON THE FRONTIER.
GALVESTON, Tex., Dec. 9.—A special dispatch from Corpus Christi to The News says: "It is rumored that a commercial traveller, well-known of this locality named Burman, and his man, have been killed near it Grande City." MONTGOMERY, Ala., Dec. 9.—A few nights ago W. Cumm, a merchant in Chambers County, was called up by a party of negroes, who alleged that they wanted to make some purchases. As soon as he opened his door he was struck down by them and killed. It is supposed that the actual murderer has beenlynched.

ELECTION ECHOES.
There was an ugly sequel to Oliver Dockery's speech at Wadesboro. A negro named Tom Wilson was arrested by Policemen Bruner and Brower for an indecency on the street, and violation of town laws. He resisted and snapped a pistol once or twice at the officers. They knocked him senseless with their clubs. A mob of negroes rushed upon them, with cries for blood and murder. The policemen fled into their dwellings, but would have been dragged out, and killed, had not Sheriff T. J. Hardison bravely faced the mob and held them in check till Marshal Tomlinson with an armed posse came to the rescue. Judge R. Tyler Bennett, also, appeared on horseback and commanded the peace. By his efforts the two policemen were brought to the court house and lodged in jail for the night to allow the drunken negroes to disperse and cool off. If the ringleaders be not arrested, and set to breaking rock on the Western N. C. R. R., the town of Wadesboro should repeal all law, and dismiss her police. The negro, Wilson, was not badly hurt, and walked home several miles in the country after the affray. So says the Times.
